name: Lejour vertical reduction

card.summary: A breast reduction technique that leaves a vertical (lollipop-shaped) scar instead of the longer anchor scar, used to bring breast size and shape into proportion with the frame.
card.aka: Lejour-Lassus, vertical mammaplasty, lollipop breast reduction
card.note: Surgical procedure with the usual operative risks, including nipple-areola complication, asymmetry and revision; performed by plastic surgeons.

quick.overview:
The Lejour vertical reduction is a form of breast reduction surgery named after Belgian plastic surgeon Madeleine Lejour. Tissue is removed through a scar that runs around the areola and straight down to the breast crease, rather than along the crease as well. Patients and surgeons who favour it describe the goal as a smaller, higher, rounder breast with a shorter scar.

Published comparisons with the older Wise-pattern (anchor) reduction describe both advantages and trade-offs. Surgeons report shorter scars and good projection, while also noting a learning curve and some risk of lower-edge irregularities that may need a touch-up.
quick.how: The operation is performed by a plastic surgeon under general anaesthesia. Excess breast tissue and skin are removed, the nipple-areola complex is kept on a tissue pedicle and moved higher, and the skin is gathered into a vertical closure. Surgeons often combine it with liposuction. Gathered skin at the base of the vertical scar commonly relaxes over the following months.
quick.risks: Reported complications include delayed wound healing, haematoma, fat necrosis, infection, partial nipple-areola loss, changed nipple sensation, asymmetry and revision surgery. Risk is described as higher with smoking, obesity and very large resections. Results vary by surgeon and patient.

lead: The Lejour vertical reduction, also called the Lejour-Lassus technique or vertical mammaplasty, is a breast reduction method in which the surgical scar encircles the areola and runs vertically down to the breast crease, without a long horizontal scar along the fold. People choose breast reduction to bring chest size into proportion with the rest of the body and to ease the weight of large breasts; it is also used to reshape and lift. Compared with the anchor-pattern (Wise) approach, the vertical approach aims to give a shorter scar and a rounder, more projecting shape.[1][2]

Plastic surgeons developed the technique in the 1990s from the work of Madeleine Lejour and earlier vertical-scar methods. A 1999 paper described modifications meant to simplify the operation and make it more reliable, noting that vertical reduction had been slow to gain acceptance in North America partly because of a perceived learning curve and a belief that it suited only smaller reductions.[1]

A 2005 comparative study of LeJour and Wise-pattern reductions examined photographs, operative times, blood loss, complications and a patient questionnaire in 112 women with moderate to large reductions.[2]

angle.text: The procedure directly reduces breast volume and lifts the breast, changing silhouette and proportion. Those who prefer it cite the shorter scar and rounder, more projecting shape compared with anchor-pattern reduction.

paras: In the vertical technique the surgeon removes breast tissue mainly from the lower and outer portions, keeps the nipple-areola complex attached to a pedicle, and closes the breast by bringing the pillars of tissue together in the vertical line. The skin initially looks gathered or puckered at the lower end of the scar; surgeons generally report that this relaxes over weeks to months, and a minority of patients have revision.[1][3]

The anchor (Wise) pattern, by contrast, adds a horizontal incision along the breast crease, giving a longer scar. Descriptions of the alternatives also include horizontal-only, periareolar and liposuction-only reductions.[3]

Authors of a 1999 paper described a simplified vertical mammaplasty meant to shorten the learning curve and make the procedure more dependable, addressing the idea that the technique was mainly suited to small reductions.[1] Later modified versions add short horizontal incisions along the fold when there is a lot of redundant skin in very large breasts.[3]

A 2005 study in Annals of Plastic Surgery compared LeJour vertical and Wise-pattern reductions in 112 women with resections above 500 g per breast, reviewing photographs, operative time, blood loss, complications and a patient questionnaire. Supporters of the vertical method had argued its shape and scar were superior, which the study set out to examine.[2]

A summary of the literature in the encyclopedia article on breast reduction reports, citing the same comparison, fewer wound-healing and infection problems with the vertical technique but more lower-edge asymmetry, with revision rates reported up to about 10 percent.[3]

General breast reduction complications described in the literature include seroma, wound separation, haematoma, partial loss of nipple-areola tissue (about 7 percent of breasts in one 1999 vertical series), reduced nipple sensation and, rarely, loss of sensation. Smoking, obesity and large resections are associated with higher risk.[3]

timeline.event: A paper describes a simplified vertical reduction mammaplasty to shorten the learning curve.[1]
A comparison of LeJour and Wise-pattern reductions is published.[2]
